content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors argue that a fully dynamic network exists with a subset of dynamic mode parameters that are redundant for performance improvement. Inspired by research in neuroscience, the authors attempt to partition a subset of static mode parameters from the fully dynamic network. This paper proposes the Partially Dynamic Network (PAD-Net) that progressively transforms less important dynamic parameters into static ones by the Iterative Mode Partition (IMP) algorithm. The authors iteratively transform dynamic parameters and measure the influence on the loss values. A dynamic parameter can be transformed into a static parameter if its transformation causes only a minimal difference in the loss value. Then they use a given dynamic ratio to balance the trade-off between dynamic and static parameters. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PAD-Net.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper attempts to answer whether all dynamic parameters in the fully dynamic network are responsible for performance improvement. The authors use the method proposed in SNIP [1] to find a minimal subset of dynamic networks that results in performance improvement and then replace those redundant dynamic parameters with static ones. This approach avoids performance degradation due to directly pruning the dynamic parameters in dynamic networks.
[1] Namhoon Lee, Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan, and Philip Torr. "SNIP: Single-shot Network Pruning based on Connection Sensitivity." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper directly applies the network pruning method SNIP [1] to dynamic networks for determining whether a dynamic parameter is redundant or not. Its contribution may be limited due to the existence of some issues that need to be clarified.
(1)	The authors try to imitate the mathematical form used in SNIP [1] (from Eq. 5 to Eq. 9), but there are some errors. For example, Eq. 7, which is the core formula of the IMP algorithm, should calculate the partial derivative of L with respect to M_j, but the formula is written as M. Moreover, the condition of t=1 is not reasonable for this formula. In addition, what is the relationship between t and t_j? 
(2)	According to Table 3, the performance of the proposed method on ImageNet without scaled factors is 77.1, which is lower than the 77.2 of DY-Conv in Table 1 under the same conditions, implying that the core IMP algorithm in this paper is not the key factor that leads to the SOTA performance of PAD-Net (77.8). A similar problem also exists on MoE, where the two learnable parameters lead to a greater improvement in the performance of the proposed method. Do these things indicate that the proposed IMP algorithm plays a weak role in the performance of the model？
(3)	Why is the sum of the two scale factors constrained to be 2 and what happens in the case where the sum of the two scale factors is 1? Furthermore, how do the values of these two scale factors change as the training progresses?
(4)	For dynamic networks such as MoE, is it reasonable to partition dynamic and static modes early in network training or even before training? How do the authors ensure that every expert in MoE is adequately trained early in the training phase?
(5)	The authors replaced some dynamic experts in MoE with static networks by the IMP algorithm, which would make these insufficiently trained experts never work. What is the difference in performance and number of parameters between PAD-Net (8 experts, top-2, dynamic ratio of 50%) and the fully dynamic network MoE (4 experts, top-2)?
(6)	In Figure 4, what is the layer-wise dynamic ratio distribution if the overall dynamic ratio is k=100% as well as k>90%? Does it still support the proposed Cherry Hypothesis?
(7)	In Figure 5 (b), why does the output variance of the dynamic network not change significantly at different layers?
(8)	How is the Mode Partition (MP) in Figure 6 implemented? Why is its performance better than dynamic networks?
(9)	According to Figure 7, at deeper layers, MoE has a higher proportion of dynamic modes. For a model that uses only static structures in the shallow layers and fully dynamic structures in the deeper layers, how would its performance compare to the proposed PAD-Net?
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper is generally well written, the novelty is somewhat limited. Please clarify the difference between the proposed method and SNIP.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to convert some of the parameters in a dynamic neural network to be static. The authors hypothesized that such conversion, if done properly, can maintain or exceed the performance of the dynamic network. The authors provide a definition of such network (Partially Dynamic Network) and a method to obtain such hybrid network (Iterative Mode Partition). This paper also provides experiments on CV (resnet, image classification) and NLP (bert-base, GLUE), showing that PAD can achieve comparable or better performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. Extensive experiments to compare the proposed method with baselines on two datasets and multiple architectures. The experiments do show comparable or better performance using the proposed method.

2. The proposed method by converting part of the dynamic network to static is new. The author demonstrate that such method can actually benefits performance. And some more analysis are provided to study the impact of the extent of the dynamic/static split. This content is useful for an initial study of this direction.

Weakness:

The proposed methods are mostly motivated by this hypothesis "A fully dynamic network contains a subset of dynamic parameters that when transforming other dynamic parameters into static ones, can maintain or even exceed the performance of the original network." This hypothesis is validated by the experiments. This hypothesis is intuitive, because that there must be some redundancy in dynamic parametrs and replacing them (properly) can at least maintain performance. Although I am grateful that the authors validate such hypothesis, I think the more important contributions should be *how* to achieve such status of a hybrid of dynamic parameters and static parameters; and the analysis of the design choices. However the "how" and the analysis in the paper gives me quite some concerns:

1. From the paper, it is a bit unclear how the IMP is trained exactly. Specifically, do we use the pre-trained dynamic network to initiate the network before using IMP? From some part, I saw the authors mentioned "We execute partition at the beginning of the second epoch". It is quite confusing. but anyhow, it looks like the PED net training needs to train the dynamic network first and then converting it to partially dynamic. It then requires a complex multi-step training process, making it quite not pratical to use. (if I understand the process wrongly, I hope the authors could clarify the training process by high-level pseudo-code, specifying clearly the input (such as pretrained weights etc)).

2. The analysis of the proposed method gives some strange results that make me worried about the effectivenss. For example, in ablation study 5.2 - dynamic ratio. It looks like dynamic ratio 10% to 50% has very small impact on the performance (up to 0.4% difference). What happens if dynamic ratio goes from 50% to 100%? Do we also see such small difference? Does it mean that the split between dynamic/static has small impact on performance? 

3. The authors do not claim for efficiency. I still want to point out that this method, even though has less parameters compared to dynamic networks, but do not have memory/computation reduction effect because the full weight matrix is still needed despite not all units are used. (considering the small flops drop negligible).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty: the proposed method is new.
Clarity of the paper is not very good. The details of the main algorithm IMP in 4.2 is unclear.
Reproducibility: The author have given the source code in the supplementary.
content.summary_of_the_review: Thank the authors to propose this new idea and provide extensive experiments to support it. However as I mentioned, there lacks some clarity of the main algorithm. And from my current understanding of the paper, I have some concerns to pratically use the proposed method, as well as some concerns regarding the effectiveness of the method. I am leaning to reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Motivated by the fact in brain science that some neurons are inactive while others are highly dynamic when a human is conducting an attention-based task, the authors propose to transfer some part of dynamic parameters into the static ones in dynamic neural networks so as to obtain good performance and low deployment costs. So, the authors propose an efficient framework named PAD-net, which can efficiently divide dynamic/static subnets, and the evaluation results show that it can outperform both fully dynamic networks and static networks in performance with low deployment overhead.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Based on the fact of brain science that some neurons are inactive while others are highly dynamic during an attention-based task, the authors propose the cherry hypothesis for the neural networks: transferring some dynamic parameters to static mode can maintain or exceed the performance of the original fully dynamic neural network. This hypothesis gives us a chance to achieve better performance with a lower deployment overhead in dynamic neural networks.
2. PAD-Net uses Iterative Mode Partition (IMP) to identify dynamic and static parameters. This method calculates scores and a  threshold for each dynamic parameter based on the loss when transferring it to static mode. The dynamic parameter with a score below the threshold will be changed into the static one. This mode partition method is proven to be effective in evaluation.
3. PAD-Net can constantly outperform fully dynamic neural networks and static networks in performance while achieving low deployment overhead compared to fully dynamic networks.


Weakness:
1. When designing the Iterative Mode Partition (IMP), the authors focus on the loss of changing one dynamic parameter to static mode, as shown in formulas (6) to (8). However, the loss of changing multiple dynamic parameters to static mode at one time may not be a linear combination of the loss of changing one parameter, so the author’s method of partitioning dynamic and static parameters may not be completely accurate.
2. The ablation study and detailed analysis are not very convincing. More evaluation or explanations should be added. See details as follows:
   1) In section 5.2, when exploring the dynamic ratio, the authors only enumerate five different values and claim that 30% is the best. The authors do not propose an efficient way to find dynamic ratio for a specific task.
   2) In section 5.3, the authors want to show that scaled factors with summation constraints will lead to better performance, but only show one example that the sum of scalar factors is 2. It is suggested to try different sum values to make this conclusion more convincing. 
   3) In section 5.4, when explaining dynamic property, the authors only show that PAD-Net’s parameters and output both have high variance, but the readers still do not know whether this dynamic is the reason why PAD-Net can perform better than static and fully dynamic methods.
3. Some evaluation setup is not properly stated in the evaluation section. For example, FLOP is not defined in Table1, and the calculation methods or definitions of performance metrics in Tables 2,3,4, and Fig. 3,5 are not explained in detail (specifically, the original performance metric before normalization is not defined in Fig. 3).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the article has good writing quality. However, there are some minor issues that may affect reading:
1) Some metrics/concepts are not properly clarified/defined in the evaluation section, as mentioned in the weakness part.
2) There are some grammar mistakes. For example, in conclusion, 'which significantly better performance and much fewer dynamic parameters' has grammar mistake.
This paper is an original work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, it is a novel idea to partition dynamic neural networks into dynamic and static subnets so as to improve performance and reduce deployment overhead, which is the cherry hypothesis mentioned in this paper. And the proposed system PAD-Net can really achieve good dynamic/static partition and get good performance and low overhead in evaluation. However, as mentioned in the weakness part, this paper has weaknesses in its design, and part of the evaluation is not convincing. I suggest giving the decision: marginally below the acceptance threshold, considering these weaknesses that cannot be ignored.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes PAD-Net (partially dynamic network), where parameters in dynamic networks can be switched between dynamic and static modes. The paper tries to answer the question: do all parameters in a dynamic network need to be dynamic? The authors propose an algorithm that iteratively converts dynamic parameters into static ones. Experiments on computer vision and natural language processing are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

* This paper studies a very interesting problem, namely can we switch between dynamic and static mode in dynamic networks.

* Experimental results seem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.


Weaknesses:

* The proposed method is essentially the same as importance score in model pruning literature. There are rather limited technical novelty.

* Presentation of the paper needs to be significantly improved. I have several questions:

  * The authors mentioned that “we start from a fully dynamic network and adopt an iterative strategy to transform dynamic parameters into static parameters step by step“. I think this is similar to iterative pruning, where there is a schedule that gradually increases the sparsity level. If this is the case, what is the schedule used to increase $\kappa$ in this case? If this is not the case, could you provide more details about the iterative strategy?

  * How is the number of parameters reduced? It is mentioned that “the indicator mask prunes out redundant parameters in dynamic parameters and static parameters respectively“. However, from Eq. 4, apparently all the model parameters are kept, except that some are considered dynamic and some are static. Please provide more details on how parameters are pruned according to $M$.

  * I do not fully understand the definition of static and dynamic parameters. From my understanding, all inputs are passed to static parameters, but only a subset of inputs are passed to dynamic parameters. Is this correct?

    * For dynamic convolution, suppose we have two kernels $W_1$ and $W_2$, initially the kernel for a specific input $x$ is $W(x) = \pi(x)_1 W_1 + \pi(x)_2 W_2$. Then how is $W(x)$ computed now since there are both static and dynamic parameters in the two kernels $W_1$ and $W_2$.
  
    * The same question for MoE. Suppose there are two experts $E_1$ and $E_2$, suppose $x_1$ is assigned to $E_1$ and $x_2$ is assigned to $E_2$. Then after the static-dynamic split, how will the inputs be routed if there are static parameters in both $E_1$ and $E_2$?

* I also have some questions and suggestions about the experiments

  * How is BERT turned into a MoE? Do you simply copy the FFN 8 times to construct 8 experts?

  * In Table 2, there are only results on CoLA, RTE, MRPC and STS-B. However, these datasets are very small and results are usually susceptible to hyper-parameter tuning and large variance. There should be results on other datasets, especially MNLI (which is the largest and the most representative task).

  * Also in Table 2, please provide the number of FLOPs.

  * In Table 4, which pruning method is used for MoE-P?

I will raise my score if the authors can address my concerns.

content.title: Less is More: Identifying the Cherry on the Cake for Dynamic Networks
content.abstract: Dynamic networks, e.g., Dynamic Convolution (DY-Conv) and the Mixture of Experts (MoE), have been extensively explored as they can considerably improve the model's representation power with acceptable computational cost. The common practice in implementing dynamic networks is to convert given static layers into fully dynamic ones where all parameters are dynamic (at least within a single layer) and vary with the input. Recent studies empirically show the trend that the more dynamic layers contribute to ever-increasing performance. However, such a fully dynamic setting 1) may cause redundant parameters and high deployment costs, limiting the applicability of dynamic networks to a broader range of tasks and models, and more importantly, 2) contradicts the previous discovery in the human brain that \textit{when human brains process an attention-demanding task, only partial neurons in the task-specific areas are activated by the input, while the rest neurons leave in a baseline state.} Critically, there is no effort to understand and resolve the above contradictory finding, leaving the primal question -- to make the computational parameters fully dynamic or not? -- unanswered. The main contributions of our work are challenging the basic commonsense in dynamic networks, and, proposing and validating the \textsc{cherry hypothesis} -- \textit{A fully dynamic network contains a subset of dynamic parameters that when transforming other dynamic parameters into static ones, can maintain or even exceed the performance of the original network.} Technically, we propose a brain-inspired partially dynamic network, namely PAD-Net, to transform the redundant dynamic parameters into static ones. Also, we further design Iterative Mode Partition to partition the dynamic- and static-subnet, which alleviates the redundancy in traditional fully dynamic networks. Our hypothesis and method are comprehensively supported by large-scale experiments with two typical advanced dynamic methods, i.e., DY-Conv and MoE, on both image classification and GLUE benchmarks. Encouragingly, we surpass the fully dynamic networks by $+0.7\%$ top-1 acc with only $30\%$ dynamic parameters for ResNet-50 and $+1.9\%$ average score in language understanding tasks with only $50\%$ dynamic parameters for BERT-base.

content.TL;DR: We reveal the contradiction between the human brain and dynamic networks, then propose and validate the Cherry Hypothesis to show that a partially dynamic network (PAD-Net) could advance the performance in dynamic networks.
